The industrial ovens hummed their low, steady lullaby, filling the air with the scent of yeast and burnt sugar. Elias wiped flour from his forearms, checking the clock: 3:17 AM. It was Thursday. He walked to the front counter, where a single, worn paperback lay on the glass display case, just as it had for the past six weeks. *The Shadow of the Wind*. He picked it up, feeling the familiar weight of its dog-eared pages. Usually, he simply placed it in the return bin behind the register, assuming a confused customer had mistaken the bakery’s late-night drop-box slot for a library return. But tonight, something felt different. The book was slightly warmer than the cool air of the shop.

He opened it to the bookmarked page. A folded square of lined notebook paper slipped out, fluttering to the countertop. Elias hesitated, then unfolded it. The handwriting was jagged, hurried. *I know you’re reading it. Keep going. Page 204 changes everything.* His heart hammered against his ribs, a sudden, sharp rhythm against the quiet hum of the mixers. He looked around the empty shop, the shadows stretching long across the tiled floor. No one was there. He looked back at the note, then at the book. With trembling fingers, he turned to page 204. The text blurred before his eyes. He closed the book, pressed it flat against the counter, and reached for his pen.

The oven hums its low, electric lullaby, a sound I’ve come to prefer over the silence of my empty apartment. It’s 3:17 AM. The witching hour for sourdough, not witches. I’m dusting flour off the prep table when I see it again. There, wedged between the industrial mixer and the wall, is that battered copy of *The Master and Margarita*. Same cracked spine. Same coffee stain on page forty-two. Every Thursday, like clockwork, someone slips this library book into my sanctuary. I’ve stopped asking who. Honestly, I don’t care. It’s become part of the ritual, like scoring the loaves or checking the proofing boxes.

But tonight feels different. The air smells sharper, maybe because of the rain hammering against the high windows. I pick up the book, expecting the usual emptiness, but something flutters out. A folded square of notebook paper, torn hastily from a spiral bound. My hands, still coated in a fine layer of white dust, tremble just slightly as I unfold it. The handwriting is jagged, urgent. *They know you’re here,* it reads. *Stop coming back.*

I stare at the words until they blur. The mixer clicks off, sudden and deafening in the quiet. I don’t call the police. I don’t scream. I just walk over to the trash bin, drop the note inside, and turn the dial on the oven up to four hundred and fifty degrees.

The industrial mixer hummed its low, steady drone, vibrating through the soles of Elias’s boots. Flour dust hung in the air, catching the harsh fluorescent light like suspended snow. It was 3:17 AM. The sourdough loaves rested on wooden boards, their crusts still pale and soft before the final bake. Elias wiped his hands on his apron, the fabric stiff with dried dough and sweat. He moved to the front counter to check the lock, a ritual born of paranoia rather than necessity.

There it sat. *The History of Salt*. Hardback, blue spine cracked near the hinge. It had appeared every Thursday for six weeks, always placed precisely on the glass display case beside the unsold cinnamon rolls. No library stamp indicated it belonged here. The bakery was not a branch of the municipal system. Elias picked it up. The cover felt cold. He opened it, expecting blank pages or perhaps a forgotten bookmark. Instead, a folded square of lined notebook paper slipped out, landing on the counter with a soft tap.

He unfolded it. The handwriting was jagged, pressed hard into the fiber. *You knead with your left hand dominant. Stop favoring the right. It ruins the tension.* Elias stared at the words. The mixer ticked over to the next cycle. He looked at his own hands, red-knuckled and dusted white. He closed the book. He placed it back on the glass, aligning the spine perfectly with the edge. Then he turned off the overhead light above the display, leaving the book in shadow.

The convection fans droned, a constant white noise beneath the scent of proofing dough and caramelized crust. Elias scraped dried batter from his knuckles. The digital clock read 3:17 AM. Thursday. He moved to the front counter where the worn paperback rested on the glass case. *The Shadow of the Wind*. It had appeared here for six weeks, always left near the metal slot used for after-hours catering orders. He usually tossed it into the return bin without a second thought, assuming a confused patron had mistaken the bakery for a library drop-off.

Tonight, the bookmark sat askew. A sharp, new crease marred the spine. Elias picked up the book. The pages smelled faintly of rain and old glue, distinct from the shop’s heavy yeast aroma. He opened to the marked section. A square of lined notebook paper fluttered onto the countertop. The handwriting was jagged, pressed hard into the fiber. *I know you’re reading it. Keep going. Page 204 changes everything.*

The mixer’s rhythm seemed to stutter in the sudden silence. Elias stared at the note. The shop was empty, the streetlights outside casting flat, yellow squares across the tile. He looked at the book. He turned to page 204. The text was dense, black ink on off-white paper. He closed the cover. He smoothed the jacket with his palm. Then he reached for the ballpoint pen tucked behind his ear.
